reason: These source-claim summaries conflated distinct figures or contradicted the reviewed Gill passages. Earlier exact assertions and citations remain here as superseded evidence; current assertions are in the authored transcript and final corrections.

mangaian_tangaroa.claim: Tangaroa is the first-born (elder) twin son of Vatea and Papa, the fair/yellow-haired god whose portion is all things red, set below his younger twin Rongo whom Vatea favoured.

citations.reference: William Wyatt Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876), Ch. I, pp. 12–14

mangaian_tangaroa.claim: When the Mangaians first saw white men they supposed them children of the fair-haired Tangaroa.

citations.reference: Robert D. Craig, Dictionary of Polynesian Mythology (1989), s.v. 'Tangaroa'

mangaian_tonga_iti.claim: Tonga-iti (Motoro), the lizard-god, is a son of Vatea and Papa and one of the tribal gods of Mangaia, a younger brother of Rongo.

citations.reference: William Wyatt Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876), Ch. I, pp. 12–14

mangaian_tonga_iti.claim: Under the name Motoro he was a chief tutelary god of the soil of Mangaia, revered by the Ngariki and manifest in the lizard.

citations.reference: Robert D. Craig, Dictionary of Polynesian Mythology (1989), s.v. 'Motoro / Tonga-iti'

mangaian_ina.claim: Ina (Ina-moe-aitu), the Mangaian Hina, beats out tapa in the moon (her cloths the clouds, her mallet the thunder) and is the heroine of the Tuna-eel tale from which the first coconut sprang.

citations.reference: William Wyatt Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876), Ch. V and the Tuna / coconut myth, pp. 77–88

mangaian_ina.claim: Ina is the woman in the moon of Mangaian belief, eternally beating bark-cloth.

citations.reference: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology (1916), pp. 88–90
